purpose: Public-domain Brenton verse-boundary reference for preserving Frenkel Hebrew wording under Brenton numbering. No Hartom text, boundaries, or modern copyrighted translation used.

englishSource.title: Brenton Septuagint Translation — Epistle of Jeremy 1
englishSource.rightsStatement: Published in 1851, and now in the Public Domain.
englishSource.editionNote: The original Brenton eBible edition (eng-Brenton), not eng-lxx2012 or Updated Brenton. The rights page dates its source files 12 Dec 2025.

printedSource.title: The Septuagint version of the Old Testament and Apocrypha : with an English translation and with various readings and critical notes
printedSource.yearNote: Internet Archive catalogs this particular scanned copy as 1900. Do not describe this scan as a verified 1851 or 1870 printing.
printedSource.creator: Brenton, Lancelot Charles Lee, Sir, 1807–1862
printedSource.layout: Printed Greek and English in parallel columns. Column sides alternate with page parity.

numbering: Both Greek and English columns use 73 verses. The first verse is typographically unnumbered, followed by printed 2 at the sins/captivity sentence. It is not an unnumbered introduction outside the verse sequence.

opening.english: A copy of an epistle, which Jeremy sent unto them which were to be led captives into Babylon by the king of the Babylonians, to certify them, as it was commanded him of God.

ending.english: Better therefore is the just man that hath no idols: for he shall be far from reproach.

boundaryObservations: All 73 English electronic-text units were visually compared with the four printed English/Greek pages for verse starts and ends. This is a boundary audit, not a claim that every Greek accent or every English letter has been independently proofread.
Verse 5 includes seeing the crowd before and behind the idols worshipping them; verse 6 begins But say ye in your hearts / Εἴπατε δὲ τῇ διανοίᾳ.

The Greek margin on page 129 groups 52,53 on the same line. English explicitly marks 52 at Who then may not know and 53 at For neither can they set up a king. Greek 53 starts Βασιλέα after the preceding question, and continues on page 130.
Verse 57 ends with the wooden/silver/gold gods unable to escape thieves or robbers; 58 starts Whose gold / ὧν οἱ ἰσχύοντες.

Verse 70 is the cucumber-garden scarecrow; 71 combines the thorn in the orchard and the dead body in darkness; 72 covers the rotting purple and later consumption/reproach; 73 is the concluding just man.
Greek margin labels indicate the line in which a verse starts, not necessarily the first word of that line. Sentence and English-column alignment were used to locate the actual word boundary.
The older CCEL electronic Brenton LJE page is empty and was not used as text evidence. The modern CCEL project says it adjusts order to Swete; it was not used to impose numbering.

scratchEvidence.rawOCRStatus: Locator only; not approved text. Printed images control boundary verification.

limitations: This report approves the Brenton reference boundaries only. The Hebrew Frenkel source, its full pointed transcription, and each Hebrew-to-Brenton correspondence require separate verification.
Greek incipits and explicits are short locating anchors, not a complete publishable Greek transcription.
